'''Abhay Ashtekar''' (born July 5, 1949) is an Indian-American theoretical physicist known for his work on [[general relativity]], [[quantum gravity]], and [[cosmology]].<ref name=":0">{{cite web | url=http://www.freepressjournal.in/world/indian-american-professor-abhay-ashtekar-wins-einstein-prize-7-facts-about-the-physicist/1378066 | title=Indian American professor Abhay Ashtekar wins Einstein prize, 7 facts about the physicist }}</ref> He is Atherton Professor, Evan Pugh University Professor, and the Eberly Chair in Physics Emeritus at [[Pennsylvania State University]].<ref name=":1">{{cite web|title=Institute for Gravitation and the Cosmos|url=https://igc.psu.edu|access-date=12 September 2024}}</ref> He also holds Distinguished Visiting Chair appointments at the [[Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics]] in Canada and the [[Raman Research Institute]] in India.<ref name=":2">{{cite web|title=Center for Fundamental Theory|url=https://cft.igc.psu.edu|access-date=12 September 2024}}</ref>

Ashtekar is the originator of the ''[[Ashtekar variables]]'', a reformulation of general relativity that led to the development of [[loop quantum gravity]]. He has contributed extensively to loop quantum gravity and its cosmological application, [[loop quantum cosmology]].<ref name=":1" /> His research has addressed the asymptotic structure of spacetime, [[gravitational wave]]s in nonlinear general relativity, [[quantum geometry]] at the [[Planck scale]], black hole physics, and the quantum description of the [[Big Bang]].<ref name=":2" />

He has authored or co-authored approximately 300 scientific papers and written or edited nine scholarly books. He has delivered more than 200 plenary lectures at international conferences and workshops.<ref name=":0" />

Ashtekar is a member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences]] and a recipient of the [[Einstein Prize (APS)|Einstein Prize]] of the [[American Physical Society]]. From 1993 to 2021, he served as the founding director of the Institute for Gravitation and the Cosmos at Penn State.<ref name=":3">{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1999/04/20/science/scientist-at-work-abhay-ashtekar-taste-testing-a-recipe-for-the-cosmos.html?pagewanted=3|title=Science at work - page 3|newspaper=The New York Times | first=James | last=Glanz | date=20 April 1999 | access-date=23 April 2010}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1999/04/20/science/scientist-at-work-abhay-ashtekar-taste-testing-a-recipe-for-the-cosmos.html?pagewanted=1|title=Science at work - page 1|newspaper=The New York Times | first=James | last=Glanz | date=20 April 1999 | access-date=23 April 2010}}</ref><ref name=":5">{{Cite web |url=http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/may-3-2016-NAS-Election.html |title=May 3, 2016: NAS Members and Foreign Associates Elected |access-date=4 May 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160506052951/http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/may-3-2016-NAS-Election.html |archive-date=6 May 2016 }}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Ashtekar was born in Shirpur, India, on July 5, 1949. His father was a senior civil servant, and the family relocated frequently. He lived in six towns in [[Maharashtra]] before completing high school in [[Kolhapur]] in 1965. He ranked among the top 15 students in the Maharashtra State Examination and received a National Merit Scholarship.<ref name="NYT2">{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1999/04/20/science/scientist-at-work-abhay-ashtekar-taste-testing-a-recipe-for-the-cosmos.html?pagewanted=2|title=Science at work - page 2|newspaper=The New York Times | first=James | last=Glanz | date=20 April 1999 | access-date=23 April 2010}}</ref>

Although selected to attend the [[Indian Institutes of Technology]], Ashtekar chose to pursue pure science and enrolled at the Institute of Science, Bombay. He graduated with honors from the [[University of Bombay]], majoring in physics with a minor in mathematics. During this period, he was mentored by B. M. Udgaonkar and S. M. Chitre at the [[Tata Institute of Fundamental Research]]. As an undergraduate, he identified a small error in ''[[The Feynman Lectures on Physics]]'' and corresponded with [[Richard Feynman]], who acknowledged the mistake.<ref name=":4" />

== Career ==
Ashtekar developed an interest in general relativity and cosmology and applied to the [[University of Texas at Austin]]. Despite not holding a master's degree, he was admitted to the Ph.D. program in physics in 1969.<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Ashtekar |first1=Abhay |title=General Relativity and Gravitation: A Centennial Perspective |date=2014 |last2=Berger |first2=Beverly K. |last3=Isenberg |first3=James |last4=MacCallum |first4=Malcolm A. H. |class=gr-qc |eprint=1409.5823 }}</ref> He worked under the supervision of [[Robert Geroch]] and later moved with him to the [[University of Chicago]], where the relativity group was led by [[Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar]]. He completed his Ph.D. in 1974.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |title=Ashtekar, Abhay on 2021 February 3. |url=https://repository.aip.org/node/129577 |website=AIP}}</ref>

He subsequently held postdoctoral positions at the Mathematical Institute, [[University of Oxford]], working with [[Roger Penrose]], and at the [[Enrico Fermi Institute]] at the University of Chicago.<ref name=":3" /> At Oxford, he developed an algebraic approach to quantum field theory in curved spacetime and, with Richard Hansen, analyzed the asymptotic structure of the gravitational field.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sacco |first=Laurent |date=2023-01-11 |title=La cosmologie quantique à boucles bientôt démontrée ? Les explications de Abhay Ashtekar |url=https://www.futura-sciences.com/sciences/actualites/astronomie-cosmologie-quantique-boucles-bientot-demontree-explications-abhay-ashtekar-101743/ |access-date=2026-02-26 |website=Futura |language=fr-FR}}</ref>

=== Academic appointments ===
Ashtekar joined the [[University of Clermont-Ferrand]] in France as ''Professeur Associé'', where he worked on gravitational waves and introduced elements of asymptotic quantization.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ashtekar |first1=Abhay |last2=Dray |first2=Tevian |date=1981-12-01 |title=On the existence of solutions to Einstein's equation with non-zero Bondi news |journal=Communications in Mathematical Physics |language=en |volume=79 |issue=4 |pages=581–599 |doi=10.1007/BF01209313 |bibcode=1981CMaPh..79..581A |issn=1432-0916}}</ref> In 1980, he was appointed Assistant Professor at [[Syracuse University]] under a [[National Science Foundation]] initiative. He was promoted to Associate Professor in 1982, Professor in 1984, [[Distinguished professor|Distinguished Professor]] in 1988, and Erastus Franklin Holden Professor in 1992.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Awards |first=Global Energy |date=2024-10-16 |title=Abhay Ashtekar {{!}} Gravitational Waves {{!}} Best Researcher Award |url=https://globalenergyawards.org/abhay-ashtekar-gravitational-waves-best-researcher-award/ |access-date=2026-02-26 |website=Global Energy Awards |language=en-GB}}</ref>

In 1983, he accepted an appointment to the ''Chaire de Gravitation'', at [[Pierre et Marie Curie University|Pierre et Marie Curie Université]], in Paris, but chose to return to Syracuse University in 1986.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kaufman |first=Ron |title=Physicist To Move From Syracuse To Penn State To Head New Center |url=https://www.the-scientist.com/physicist-to-move-from-syracuse-to-penn-state-to-head-new-center-59827 |access-date=2026-02-26 |website=The Scientist |language=en}}</ref>

In 1993, Ashtekar joined Pennsylvania State University as Eberly Chair in Physics and established a new Center for Gravitation. In 1999, he declined an offer of a Directorship at the [[Max Planck Institute]] for Gravitational Physics in Germany. He has remained at Penn State since 1993.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Ramesh |first=Sandhya |date=2018-10-17 |title=Mumbai physicist who devised mathematical way to define Einstein prediction wins top prize |url=https://theprint.in/science/mumbai-physicist-who-devised-mathematical-way-to-define-einstein-prediction-wins-top-prize/135931/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230327041115/https://theprint.in/science/mumbai-physicist-who-devised-mathematical-way-to-define-einstein-prediction-wins-top-prize/135931/ |archive-date=2023-03-27 |access-date=2026-02-26 |work=ThePrint |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Institute for Gravitation and the Cosmos ===
In 2001, Ashtekar chaired the executive committee of a second Center at Penn State focused on Gravitational Wave Physics. It was funded by the National Science Foundation in the very first year of their Physics Frontier Centers initiative.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2018-10-16 |title=Einstein Prize-winning Indo-American Professor Abhay Ashtekar talks gravity, physics- Technology News, Firstpost |url=https://www.firstpost.com/tech/science/einstein-prize-winning-indo-american-professor-abhay-ashtekar-talks-gravity-physics-5387871.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200802190709/https://www.firstpost.com/tech/science/einstein-prize-winning-indo-american-professor-abhay-ashtekar-talks-gravity-physics-5387871.html |archive-date=2020-08-02 |access-date=2026-02-26 |work=Tech2 |language=en-US}}</ref>

The two centers became part of the Institute for Gravitation and the Cosmos (IGC), which expanded to include cosmology and multimessenger astronomy and astrophysics.  Ashtekar served as director of the IGC and its predecessor centers from 1993 until stepping down in 2021.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-02-11 |title=Gravitational waves detected 100 years after Einstein's prediction {{!}} Penn State University |url=https://www.psu.edu/news/research/story/gravitational-waves-detected-100-years-after-einsteins-prediction |access-date=2026-02-26 |website=www.psu.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-10-07 |title=Nobel winner Penrose has long-standing ties to Penn State {{!}} Penn State University |url=https://www.psu.edu/news/research/story/nobel-winner-penrose-has-long-standing-ties-penn-state |access-date=2026-02-26 |website=www.psu.edu}}</ref>

== Research ==

=== Classical general relativity ===
Ashtekar's work in classical general relativity includes studies of the asymptotic structure of spacetime, [[gravitational radiation]], and [[black hole]] dynamics. With collaborators including Richard Hansen and Anne Magnon, he identified the asymptotic symmetry group at spatial infinity, known as the Spi group, and analyzed associated conserved quantities, especially the subtleties in the notion of angular momentum of space-times with gravitational waves.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ashtekar |first1=Abhay |last2=Hansen |first2=R. O. |date=1978-07-01 |title=A unified treatment of null and spatial infinity in general relativity. I. Universal structure, asymptotic symmetries, and conserved quantities at spatial infinity |url=https://pubs.aip.org/jmp/article/19/7/1542/454072/A-unified-treatment-of-null-and-spatial-infinity |journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics |language=en |volume=19 |issue=7 |pages=1542–1566 |doi=10.1063/1.523863 |bibcode=1978JMP....19.1542A |issn=0022-2488|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Schneider |first1=Berend |last2=Khera |first2=Neev |date=2025-11-12 |title=From spatial to null infinity: Connecting initial data to peeling |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/hcx1-hcf9 |journal=Physical Review D |language=en |volume=112 |issue=10 |article-number=104024 |doi=10.1103/hcx1-hcf9 |arxiv=2507.07977 |bibcode=2025PhRvD.112j4024S |issn=2470-0010}}</ref>

His research on gravitational waves demonstrated that their physical content is encoded in the curvature of a connection defined on Penrose's conformal boundary of [[spacetime]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-09-10 |title=Black holes everywhere! Ten years of LIGO and gravitational waves {{!}} Penn State University |url=https://www.psu.edu/news/eberly-college-science/story/black-holes-everywhere-ten-years-ligo-and-gravitational-waves |access-date=2026-02-26 |website=www.psu.edu}}</ref> These ideas provided the foundation for later work on infrared effects, gravitational memory and [[celestial holography]] and recent efforts to improve gravitational waveform modeling for [[LIGO Scientific Collaboration|LIGO–Virgo]] data analysis.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-09-14 |title=Prof. Abhay Ashtekar in conversation with Prof. Martin Hendry |url=https://www.ligo-india.in/2-abhay/ |access-date=2026-02-26 |website=LIGO-India |language=en-US}}</ref>

Ashtekar and collaborators, including Badri Krishnan introduced quasi-local horizons, including isolated and dynamical horizons, which are now widely used in numerical simulations of black hole formation and mergers, and in investigations of the black hole evaporation due to emission of quantum radiation discovered by [[Stephen Hawking]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ashtekar |first1=Abhay |title=Quasi-local black hole horizons: Recent advances |date=2025-07-28 |arxiv=2502.11825 |last2=Krishnan |first2=Badri |journal=Living Reviews in Relativity |volume=28 |issue=1 |article-number=8 |doi=10.1007/s41114-025-00061-4 |bibcode=2025LRR....28....8A }}</ref> He has also studied asymptotic properties of gravitational fields in spacetimes with nonzero cosmological constant.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ashtekar |first1=Abhay |title=Asymptotics with a positive cosmological constant: I. Basic framework |date=2014-10-17 |last2=Bonga |first2=Beatrice |last3=Kesavan |first3=Aruna |journal=Classical and Quantum Gravity |volume=32 |issue=2 |article-number=025004 |doi=10.1088/0264-9381/32/2/025004 |arxiv=1409.3816 }}</ref>

=== Quantum gravity and Ashtekar variables ===
Ashtekar's research on quantum gravity began with work on quantum field theory in curved spacetime, including algebraic and Kähler-geometric methods. In the 1980s, he developed a non-perturbative quantization of the radiative modes of gravity and identified connections between infrared issues and asymptotic symmetries.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Ashtekar |first=Abhay |year=1987 |title=New Hamiltonian formulation of general relativity |journal=Physical Review D |volume=36 |issue=6 |pages=1587–1602 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.36.1587 |pmid=9958340 |bibcode=1987PhRvD..36.1587A }}</ref>

In 1986, he reformulated general relativity using self-dual connections, now known as ''Ashtekar variables''. This reformulation simplified Einstein's equations and cast general relativity in a gauge-theoretic form, enabling the development of loop quantum gravity.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ashtekar |first1=Abhay |last2=Rovelli |first2=Carlo |last3=Smolin |first3=Lee |date=1992 |title=Self duality and quantization |url=https://www.scopus.com/pages/publications/1642356223 |journal=Journal of Geometry and Physics |volume=8 |issue=1–4 |pages=7–27 |doi=10.1016/0393-0440(92)90041-X |arxiv=hep-th/9202079 |bibcode=1992JGP.....8....7A |issn=0393-0440}}</ref>

In 2011, the international conference ''Loops 11: Celebrating 25 Years of Loop Quantum Gravity'' was held in [[Madrid]] to commemorate the 25th anniversary of Ashtekar's landmark paper introducing the variables that helped launch the loop quantum gravity research program.<ref>{{cite web |title=25th Anniversary of Ashtekar's Landmark Paper is Honored at Conference in Spain {{!}} Eberly College of Science |url=https://science.psu.edu/news/25th-anniversary-ashtekars-landmark-paper-honored-conference-spain |website=science.psu.edu}}</ref>

=== Loop quantum gravity and cosmology ===
Loop quantum gravity predicts a quantum geometry in which geometric operators corresponding to area and volume have discrete spectra.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rovelli |first1=Carlo |last2=Smolin |first2=Lee |year=1995 |title=Discreteness of area and volume in quantum gravity |journal=Nuclear Physics B |volume=442 |issue=3 |pages=593–619 |doi=10.1016/0550-3213(95)00150-Q |arxiv=gr-qc/9411005 |bibcode=1995NuPhB.442..593R }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ashtekar |first1=Abhay |last2=Lewandowski |first2=Jerzy |year=1997 |title=Quantum theory of geometry I: Area operators |journal=Classical and Quantum Gravity |volume=14 |issue=1A |pages=A55–A82 |doi=10.1088/0264-9381/14/1A/006 |arxiv=gr-qc/9602046 |bibcode=1997CQGra..14A..55A }}</ref> The theory was further developed by numerous researchers, including Ivan Agullo, [[Jerzy Lewandowski]], [[Carlo Rovelli]], [[Lee Smolin]], and Thomas Thiemann, many of whom are former members of Ashtekar's research group, and by their own students.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ashtekar |first1=Abhay |last2=Lewandowski |first2=Jerzy |year=2004 |title=Background independent quantum gravity: A status report |journal=Classical and Quantum Gravity |volume=21 |issue=15 |pages=R53–R152 |doi=10.1088/0264-9381/21/15/R01 |arxiv=gr-qc/0404018 }}</ref>

In loop quantum cosmology, Ashtekar and collaborators showed that quantum geometric effects resolve the classical Big Bang singularity, replacing it with a cosmological bounce.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ashtekar |first1=Abhay |last2=Pawlowski |first2=Tomasz |last3=Singh |first3=Parampreet |year=2006 |title=Quantum Nature of the Big Bang |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=96 |issue=14 |article-number=141301 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.96.141301 |pmid=16712061 |arxiv=gr-qc/0602086 |bibcode=2006PhRvL..96n1301A }}</ref> They also showed that these quantum geometric effects can modify the evolution of primordial perturbations and may leave observable imprints in the cosmic microwave background, potentially accounting for certain large-scale anomalies.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Agullo |first1=Ivan |last2=Ashtekar |first2=Abhay |last3=Nelson |first3=William |year=2012 |title=Quantum Gravity Extension of the Inflationary Scenario |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=109 |issue=25 |article-number=251301 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.109.251301 |pmid=23368448 |arxiv=1209.1609 |bibcode=2012PhRvL.109y1301A }}</ref>

In black hole physics, loop quantum gravity provides a microscopic account of black hole entropy.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Rovelli |first=Carlo |year=1996 |title=Black hole entropy from loop quantum gravity |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=77 |issue=16 |pages=3288–3291 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.77.3288 |pmid=10062183 |arxiv=gr-qc/9603063 |bibcode=1996PhRvL..77.3288R }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ashtekar |first1=Abhay |last2=Baez |first2=John |last3=Corichi |first3=Alejandro |last4=Krasnov |first4=Krzysztof |year=1998 |title=Quantum geometry and black hole entropy |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=80 |issue=5 |pages=904–907 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.80.904 |arxiv=gr-qc/9710007 |bibcode=1998PhRvL..80..904A }}</ref> It has also been applied to the study of black hole evaporation through frameworks based on quantum geometry and quasi-local or isolated horizons.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ashtekar |first1=Abhay |last2=Krishnan |first2=Badri |year=2004 |title=Isolated and dynamical horizons and their applications |journal=Living Reviews in Relativity |volume=7 |issue=1 |article-number=10 |doi=10.12942/lrr-2004-10 |doi-access=free |pmid=28163644 |pmc=5253930 |arxiv=gr-qc/0407042 |bibcode=2004LRR.....7...10A }}</ref>

== Outreach, service, and mentoring ==
Ashtekar founded the ''Frontiers of Science'' public lecture series at Penn State, which has been held annually for more than three decades and was renamed the ''Ashtekar Lectures on Frontiers of Science'' in 2020.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ashtekar Frontiers of Science {{!}} Eberly College of Science |url=https://science.psu.edu/frontiers |access-date=2026-02-26 |website=science.psu.edu}}</ref>

He has served as President of the [[International Society on General Relativity and Gravitation]] and as Chair of the Division of [[Gravitational physics|Gravitational Physics]] of the [[American Physical Society]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Institute for Gravitation and the Cosmos {{!}} Abhay Ashtekar |url=https://igc.psu.edu/people/bio/ava1/ |access-date=2026-02-26 |website=igc.psu.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Abhay Ashtekar |url=https://physics.aps.org/authors/abhay_ashtekar |website=APS}}</ref> He has served on editorial boards of major journals and was Editor-in-Chief of ''General Relativity and Gravitation: A Centenary Perspective''.<ref name=":5" />

The [[American Institute of Physics]] conducted an oral history interview with Ashtekar for the Niels Bohr Library in 2021.<ref name=":6" /> He has mentored over 100 postdocs and graduate students including;<ref name="Rediff on the Net">{{cite web|url=http://www.rediff.com/news/1999/may/15us5.htm|title=Dr. Abhay Ashtekar|publisher=Rediff on the Net}}</ref>
